title: Knowledge Check 10: Lessons 73-75
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 73-75 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per lesson 73, why should you run the platform on cost per completed task rather than cost per token?
options: Because cost per token is a vanity metric: per-token prices keep falling while total bills keep rising, since the work-per-task multiplier grows faster than the price per unit comes down, and a per-token view hides expensive output tokens and retries
Because cost per token is always higher and easier for finance to negotiate down
Because cost per token does not exist as a metric in any provider's invoice
Because cost per completed task only includes the model output and ignores all input tokens
questions.explanation: The lesson states cost per token is a vanity metric: per-million-token prices keep falling while enterprise AI bills still rise, because agentic workflows grow the work-per-task multiplier faster than the price per unit falls. A per-token view also hides expensive output tokens and retries. The unit that actually governs money is cost per completed task, traced across every input, output, retry, and sub-agent step.

questions.question: A team cuts per-call context size by 40% but the change triggers 67% more model calls. Using the lesson's three-lever cost identity, why does this fail to save money?
options: Because the routing classifier always spends more tokens than the context it saved

Because a 40% reduction in context multiplied by a 67% increase in calls reaches roughly break-even under the linear cost model, so the save on lever one is spent back on lever two, the call count, and each added call also retransmits the growing context on every turn
Because reducing context size automatically increases output tokens by the same amount
Because prompt caching is disabled whenever the context changes, wiping out all savings
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Infosys: a 40% reduction in per-call context that triggers 67% more calls reaches break-even under the linear cost model, because 0.60 multiplied by 1.67 is approximately 1.00. The interaction compounds because each added call retransmits accumulated history rather than a fixed-size payload. This is the substitution effect the lesson warns about: naive optimizations shift cost between levers rather than removing it.

questions.question: A team wants to move a workload from a managed LLM API to self-hosted GPU infrastructure. Per lesson 73, what is the correct economic decision rule?
options: Self-host whenever the workload is narrow, because narrow tasks always justify fixed hardware
Never self-host, because managed APIs are always cheaper than owning GPUs
Decide on enthusiasm for open-source models rather than measured volume

Model the crossover against metering data and move the workload only when sustained GPU utilization clears roughly 60% to 70%, because below about 30% utilization self-hosting is usually more expensive than the API and the economics only tilt sharply in favor of self-hosting at high utilization
questions.explanation: The lesson applies a utilization threshold: on dedicated GPU inference, below roughly 30% realized utilization self-hosting is frequently more expensive than the API alternative, and above 60% to 70% utilization the economics tilt sharply toward self-hosting. The strategic move is to use telemetry to identify the highest-volume, narrowest tasks and move only those, and to start self-hosting only after metering confirms enough volume and utilization to justify the fixed infrastructure spend.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, why does a security review for an agent have to start with assets and never-boundaries rather than jumping straight to the attack list?
options: Because the attack list is the same for every agent and needs no local context

Because you cannot decide what to protect against a threat until you have said what that threat is meant to reach, and the asset list in an AI system extends beyond databases to include the integrity of the context the model reasons over and the integrity of the agent's actions
Because threat modeling only cares about confidentiality of stored data
Because naming assets is optional and only matters for auditors after launch
questions.explanation: The lesson follows Microsoft's AI threat-modeling guidance: start by being explicit about what you are protecting. Assets extend beyond databases and credentials to user safety, trust, privacy, the integrity of prompts and contextual data, and the integrity of the agent's actions. The assets exercise also forces the honest question of what action the system should never take, which gives the threat set something concrete to attach to.

questions.question: A support agent can read a customer email, retrieve a policy document, update a CRM row, and call a refund tool. An attacker embeds hostile instructions inside a document the agent will retrieve. Using the lesson's threat model, why does the refund call get stopped even though the model's intent has moved?
options: Because the model's refusal training recognizes the embedded text and refuses to act
Because the retrieved document is validated and rejected before it enters the context window

Because the injection can move the model's intent but cannot override the deterministic boundaries around it: a hard verify step that requires a matching copied receipt, a support-tier identity with no refund permission, and a default-deny policy that logs every call
Because the prompt is hashed against a known-good registry and any new version is dropped
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the injection targets the model, and the defense lives in the wiring around it. The refund tool is gated behind deterministic verify logic that requires a verified matching receipt, the support-tier identity has no refund permission at all, and the gateway applies default-deny so the refund call only succeeds for the human escalation path. What stops the attack is not the model being careful; it is that the action is unachievable from where the agent sits.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, what is the most important requirement for the residual-risk column of a written security review?
options: Every threat must be mitigated so no residual risk remains
Each accepted risk gets a named owner who writes down why it is accepted, because a review that records who accepted each remaining risk is the record a governance board and auditor actually want
Residual risk is only recorded for threats above a token-spend threshold
The column is populated automatically by the vendor's security scanner
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the residual-risk column is the most important and the one most teams skip. Every accepted risk needs a name and a reason, or it is not a decision, it is an omission. A review that ends with every row mitigated is not being honest, because no agent is fully hardened. Recording who accepted each remaining risk is what makes the review an auditable system that a governance board can sign.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Incident Response for Agents", what must happen before any rollback, restart, or credential revocation when you confirm an agent incident?
options: Export or snapshot the incident window's trace tree to storage independent of the production system
Delete the affected sessions' logs so the bad behavior is not preserved
Revert to the last known-good prompt immediately to stop the bleeding
Restart the agent to clear its in-memory state before investigating
questions.explanation: The lesson: a rollback swaps the running version and a restart clears in-memory state, and either can overwrite or orphan the exact span-level record the postmortem needs. So you freeze or export the trace first, to storage independent of production, before any recovery action.

questions.question: The answer agent that made the mistake sent 40 incorrect refund emails to customers. Per the lesson's rollback-by-action-class framework, why is this class hard to roll back, and what is the correct substitute?
options: Emails are idempotent and can be reversed like a database write, so no follow-up is needed
A sent message cannot be unsent, so the response is a follow-up communication template, a legal review of that follow-up, and extraction of the impacted-customer list
The emails can be recalled because the agent has read access to the customer inboxes
Restarting the agent makes the sent emails untraceable so they can be ignored
questions.explanation: The lesson groups customer communications as the class where a sent message cannot be unsent. The rollback table specifies the substitute action: a follow-up communication template under legal review plus the impacted-customer list extraction.

questions.question: In the MTTD-for-Agents detection chain, if the entire fourteen-day delay before awareness sits between Signal and Trigger, what is the root cause you should fix, per the lesson?
options: Missing instrumentation on the agent's action path
Poor alerting hygiene, because the pager did not reach the operator
A tripwire that never fired on the signal
The human took too long to acknowledge the page
questions.explanation: The lesson maps each gap in the chain to its own root cause: a delay between Action and Signal is missing instrumentation, between Signal and Trigger is a tripwire that never fired, and between Page and Acknowledgement is alerting hygiene. Here the gap is Signal to Trigger, so the missing tripwire is the fix.
